title: Organizational Structure for Software-Defined Products
author: Uwe Mierisch
summary: Uwe Mierisch, a product development consultant, argues that the traditional hardware-centric engineering organization, in which whoever owns a part owns the problem, breaks down once software runs on a central computer and the cause of a fault is no longer obvious. He reviews three alternatives: the agile organization, which separates the what from the how and the work from people management; the Chinese centralised model, which is fast and disciplined but depends on the boss; and systems engineering, which unifies hardware and software but says nothing about people and resources. From these he proposes a system-centric organization led by a head of engineering as commander, with a chief architect owning features, system owners owning how those features are delivered, a shared resources owner, and a pooled project management unit. He adds that rank should not be measured by headcount, that bosses need their own staff, and that self-reliant employees should be rated above those who send every problem upward. The domain is automotive engineering, but the structural argument about responsibility and culture applies to any complex organization.
points: Part ownership creates a culture of defense, where the first reaction to a failure is to prove the part is not yours, and it collapses when hardware and software are interwoven.
Each rival model has one strength the others lack: agile separates the what from the how, the Chinese way decides fast, and systems engineering sees hardware and software together.
The proposed system-centric structure makes customer value, not the part, the leading dimension, with features owned once by the chief architect and the how owned by system owners.
The how at one level becomes the what and why at the next, so value flows from purpose to teams without detours and with few management layers.
Executive rank should not be counted by headcount, staff positions are a necessary resource rather than a privilege, and employees who solve their own problems should be rated higher.
quotes: A company can somehow get by with a missing strategy and bad product decisions. An unclear organizational structure brings it to a standstill.
The first reaction is almost always: It’s not my part, it’s someone else’s. Before I take responsibility, you’ll have to prove that my parts are the cause of the problem.
Separating the goal from the path is pure mission command in Moltke’s sense. The product owner decides the what and the why. The team decides the how.

The greatest weakness lies in separating responsibility for the work from responsibility for the people. Whoever decides on an employee’s development is not responsible for what that employee delivers.
The greatest weakness is dependence on the boss. The organization is only as good as the people deciding at the center.
Every known organizational form has advantages and disadvantages. My proposal tries to combine the essential advantages and soften the disadvantages as much as possible.
In many companies, an executive’s rank is measured by how many people report to them. The more people, the more important the boss.
Staff positions are often abolished today because they are seen as a privilege. They’re not a privilege. They’re a necessary resource.
